source_title: Bellbrook Flying-Fox Droppings — What's Actually Established
evidence_description: Histoplasmosis (a fungal lung/bloodstream infection from inhaling spores in accumulated droppings) is a real, medically documented mechanism. Standard "living near a flying-fox camp is low risk" council/NSW Health messaging is calibrated for distant colonies with no droppings contact - not for roofs, gutters and yards under direct heavy accumulation. No lab test has confirmed Histoplasma capsulatum in this specific colony's droppings; that would require environmental sampling not yet done. The document explicitly frames the messaging gap as a scope limitation, not a claim about anyone's intent, and notes an absence of confirmed local cases does not mean no mild/undiagnosed infections have occurred - clinical literature cited puts undiagnosed rates as high as 90% in immunocompetent people.
relevant_quotation: The illness mechanism is real; the source confirmation isn't there yet.
investigation_relevance: The health-risk dimension of the case, self-hedged at the source to distinguish established mechanism from unconfirmed local instance - matches this project's own evidentiary standard already.

investigation_relevance: The load-bearing claim for the Hardened Submission Package's SafeWork NSW and Office of Local Government submissions (Part 5), which characterise the failure as non-execution of an affirmative unanimous directive rather than a discretionary refusal. This is a materially stronger claim than the rest of the case supports as things stand. Do not use in any public-facing material until verified against the actual signed minutes. See CTR-0001, Q-0001.

source_title: NSW flying-fox grants program is plan-gated
evidence_description: The NSW Government holds approximately $1 million for councils managing flying-fox camp impacts. Access requires a completed or draft Camp Management Plan for the specific site. Without a plan, a site is not eligible - meaning Bellbrook cannot lawfully receive plan-gated funding regardless of any grant application council makes, unless directed to Rudder Park (the only site with a plan).
relevant_quotation: A Camp Management Plan is the access mechanism for state funding. Without a plan, a site is not eligible.
investigation_relevance: This is the case's core structural finding: a real remedy mechanism exists, gated behind a single document council has declined to produce. Not yet independently confirmed against the NSW Government's own grant program guidelines.

source_title: Level 1/Level 2 management actions available without a licence
evidence_description: Described consistently across two independently-toned documents: the NSW Flying-fox Camp Management Code of Practice 2018 pre-approves certain Level 1 (routine site management, hygiene cleaning, signage) and Level 2 (vegetation buffer creation, branch trimming) interventions without individual licensing, subject to welfare-based scheduling conditions (e.g. trimming after animals depart to forage). Protected-species status prevents dispersal or lethal control; it does not prevent these actions.
relevant_quotation: The legal protection applies to harming the bats. It does not apply to protecting the community from the harm the bats cause.
investigation_relevance: Directly undercuts any framing that legal protection alone explains council's inaction - the two documents differ sharply in how they characterise council's conduct (CTR-0001) but agree on what the Code of Practice actually permits. Not yet checked against the primary Code of Practice document itself.

source_authority: ABC News (Gabrielle Becerra Mellet, ABC North Qld)
source_title: North Queensland health authorities issue warning over flying foxes after more exposures
evidence_description: Reports a rise in flying-fox bite/scratch exposures in the Townsville (17 cases) and Mackay (20 cases) health districts, North Queensland, since the start of 2025. Australian bat lyssavirus (ABLV) is named as the serious risk from such exposures - potentially fatal, causing paralysis, delirium and convulsions; four deaths recorded nationally since 1996, the most recent in NSW. Health authorities state every bat bite or scratch should be treated as a possible exposure and requires immediate medical treatment (wound washing, then emergency department attendance).
relevant_quotation: ABLV is one of the most lethal viruses we know of — it can cause paralysis, delirium, convulsions and ultimately death.
investigation_relevance: Operator flagged this as relevant background, not as evidence of a Bellbrook-specific incident. Establishes a second, distinct flying-fox health-risk pathway (bite/scratch transmission of ABLV) alongside EV-0008's droppings-based histoplasmosis risk - different mechanism, different exposure route, same underlying point: real medical risks exist independent of any confirmed local case. Not specific to Bellbrook, Kempsey, or even NSW - North Queensland colonies and exposure circumstances (rescuing tangled/injured animals) differ from Bellbrook's documented droppings-contamination concern. See THR-05.

source_authority: Mid North Coast Local Health District (NSW Health)
source_title: Avoid handling bats to protect yourself against lyssavirus
evidence_description: Mid North Coast Local Health District's own general public health guidance: avoid handling or touching injured or dead flying foxes and microbats; contact wildlife rescue services for distressed animals; wash any bite/scratch wound with soap and water for 15 minutes and seek immediate medical attention; only trained, vaccinated wildlife carers should handle bats. Addresses the broader Mid North Coast region generally - does not name Kempsey, Bellbrook, or the Macleay Valley specifically.
relevant_quotation: avoid handling or touching injured or dead flying foxes and microbats
investigation_relevance: Independently fetched and read in full (2026-08-23) - the only ABLV-related item in this case that is Verified rather than Requires Verification. This is the same local health authority already named in EV-0004 (council's letter states it corresponded with Mid North Coast Local Health District regarding Bellbrook specifically) - meaning this general regional guidance sits alongside a documented, case-specific contact between council and this exact authority, though the content of that specific correspondence remains unknown (see Q-0003).

source_title: Further options to be investigated in Flying-Fox Plan
evidence_description: On 1 April 2026, Townsville City Council unanimously adopted a revised Flying-Fox Management Plan covering 16 recorded roosts, adding active dispersal as a feasibility option alongside existing routine-management and low-impact strategies - the first time dispersal has been added to that plan. The revision followed 2024 community consultation (information sessions and an online survey); most survey respondents agreed flying-foxes should be managed (60%) and that living near them was a serious problem (54%, described as "horrible"). Mayor Nick Dametto is quoted framing the change as improving Council's position to seek external funding if dispersal is found viable.
relevant_quotation: This is an incremental but important change to Council's Flying-Fox Management Plan which allows us to further investigate all management options, including dispersal.
investigation_relevance: A second, independent comparator to Rudder Park (EV-0002): a different council in a different state actively operating, consulting on, and revising a working Flying-fox Camp Management Plan in the same month this case is being investigated. Strengthens the Documented Compliance vs. Functional Compliance contrast at the centre of this case - the mechanism is not rare, difficult, or unusual to operate; multiple councils run and actively improve it. Kempsey has not reached initial plan adoption for Bellbrook, let alone active revision.
